title: Effect of Clinical Pharmacist Interventions on Blood Pressure Control
abstract: Background: Hypertension control remains suboptimal in many outpatient settings. Objective: To evaluate the impact of clinical pharmacist-led medication management on blood pressure control among adults with persistent hypertension. Methods: We conducted a prospective, randomized controlled trial across three ambulatory clinics. Adult patients with uncontrolled hypertension despite at least two antihypertensive agents were randomized to receive either pharmacist-managed care with collaborative practice agreements or usual physician-led care. Interventions included comprehensive medication review, adherence assessment, titration authority, and patient education. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients achieving target blood pressure at 6 months. Secondary outcomes included mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure change, medication adherence scores, adverse drug events, and patient satisfaction. Results: A greater proportion of patients in the pharmacist-managed arm achieved target blood pressure compared with usual care (68% vs 45%, p=0.01). Mean systolic blood pressure decreased by 18 mmHg in the intervention group versus 10 mmHg in control (p=0.02). Adverse events were similar between groups, with no serious events attributed to pharmacist interventions. Statistical analysis used intention-to-treat principles with multiple imputation for missing data. Conclusion: Clinical pharmacist-led medication management significantly improved blood pressure control without compromising safety, supporting broader implementation of collaborative practice models.
